items.passage: When Daniel moved into his new flat, he did not know anyone in the building. On his first evening, he tried to cook dinner but discovered that he had no salt. He knocked on the door opposite and asked his neighbour, an older woman named Rosa, if she could help. Rosa smiled and gave him a small bag of salt. The next day, Daniel baked some bread and took half of it to her. They now meet in the hallway almost every morning and talk about the weather, the garden or the local shops.

items.evidence: he tried to cook dinner but discovered that he had no salt.

items.passage: The town library used to close at six, which made it hard for people who worked during the day. Last month it began staying open until nine on weekdays. The library also added more desks near the windows and a small area where visitors can make tea. The librarian says the change has brought in many new readers, especially students preparing for exams. Not everyone is happy: a few residents have complained about noise in the evenings. The library is now testing a rule that asks visitors to keep phone calls outside the reading rooms.
items.question: Why did the library change its closing time?
options: To make room for a cafe.
To attract readers who work during the day.
Because students asked for fewer desks.
items.evidence: The town library used to close at six, which made it hard for people who worked during the day.

items.passage: For years, manufacturers have designed products that are difficult to repair: batteries are sealed, spare parts are scarce, and software locks out independent workshops. The "right to repair" movement argues that this wastes resources and limits consumer choice. Some governments now require companies to publish repair manuals and supply parts for a minimum number of years. Manufacturers warn that such rules could raise prices and slow innovation. Yet the debate is shifting. As electronic waste grows, the question is less about whether repair should be allowed than about who controls the knowledge required to do it.
items.question: What is the main issue?
options: Why new phones are too cheap.
Who controls the knowledge needed to repair products.
items.evidence: the question is less about whether repair should be allowed than about who controls the knowledge required to do it.

items.passage: A notification is a small interruption, but its effects are cumulative. Each alert competes for attention, and even when ignored it leaves a trace: a decision postponed, a train of thought broken. Designers defend alerts as a service to users who want to stay informed. Critics reply that many alerts serve the platform's need for engagement rather than the user's need for information. The disagreement is not really about technology. It concerns who has the right to decide what deserves our attention, and whether convenience is worth the cost of being constantly available.
items.question: What is the main argument?
options: Notifications raise questions about who controls attention.
Users should never check their phones.
items.evidence: It concerns who has the right to decide what deserves our attention
